extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and instructors in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of cup product structure (including divided polynomial algebras and realizability of polynomial cohomology rings) and the beginning of Poincaré duality: orientations, fundamental class, and local homology statements for closed manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell structure of J(S^n) and resulting homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving S^n its usual CW structure, the resulting CW structure on J(S^n) consists of exactly one cell in each dimension a multiple of n. Hence (for n>1) H^*(J(S^n);Z) consists exactly of Z's in dimensions a multiple of n (the cellular boundary maps are trivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative argument via the quotient map q:(S^n)^m→J_m(S^n): q is cellular and surjective on cells, so cellular boundary maps for J_m(S^n) are trivial when they are trivial for (S^n)^m. If n=1 handle separately via the quotient argument. This explains why cohomology has one Z in each multiple-of-n degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup-product relations in H^*(J(S^n)) for n even
rubrics_metrics.description: When n is even the cup product structure in H^*(J(S^n);Z) is strictly commutative; with x_k the generator of H^{kn}, one has q^*(x_1)=α_1+···+α_m and q^*(x_1^m)=(α_1+···+α_m)^m = m! α_1···α_m = m! q^*(x_m), hence x_1^m = m! x_m in H^*(J(S^n);Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via the map q^* from the product (S^n)^m where H^*((S^n)^m;Z) ≅ Z[α_1,...,α_m]/(α_1^2,...,α_m^2) for n even. Use that inclusion J_m(S^n)→J(S^n) induces isomorphisms on H^i for i≤mn to pass relations to the infinite symmetric product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup-product relations in H^*(J(S^n)) for n odd
rubrics_metrics.description: For n odd one has x_1^2 = 0, and the essential multiplicative relations include (a) x_1 x_{2m} = x_{2m+1} in H^*(J_{2m+1}(S^n);Z) and (b) x_2 x_{2m-2} = m x_{2m} in H^*(J_{2m}(S^n);Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove these by applying q^* and computing in the exterior algebra H^*((S^n)^m;Z) (signs from exterior multiplication give the indicated integer coefficients). These relations characterize the algebraic structure when n is odd (e.g. many squares vanish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided polynomial algebra Γ (Gamma) and its multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: The subring of the polynomial ring Q[x] additively generated by the monomials x^i/i! is called a divided polynomial algebra, denoted Γ. More generally, for a commutative ring R define R[x]_Γ to be the free R-module with basis x_0=1,x_1,x_2,... and multiplication defined so that x_i x_j = (i+j choose i) x_{i+j} (equivalently, if over Q one may rescale to get the usual polynomial multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When R=Q this recovers Q[x]; when R=Z_p (p prime) one gets a different structure: Γ⊗Z_p ≅ Z_p[x_{p^i}]/(x_{p^i}^p) (i≥0). Divided polynomial algebras are in a certain sense dual to polynomial algebras; see §3.C for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realizability of H^*(X;R) ≅ R[α] (table of allowed generator degrees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a coefficient ring R and integer d>0, ask for a space X with H^*(X;R) ≅ R[α] where |α|=d. For common choices of R the possible d are: R=Z → d=2,4; R=Q → any even number; R=Z_2 → d=1,2,4; R=Z_p (p odd) → any even divisor of 2(p-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessity that d be even when R≠Z_2 follows from graded-commutativity of cup product. Stronger restrictions are: for R=Z, d must be a power of 2; for R=Z_2, d must be a power of 2; for R=Z_p (p odd) d must be a power of p times an even divisor of 2(p-1). Some remaining cases are settled using K-theory; an exceptional case R=Z_2,d=8 requires special arguments (Toda 1963). Examples: CP^∞ (d=2), HP^∞ (d=4), and J(S^d) give Q-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of CW complexes X_d realizing polynomial cohomology for admissible d
rubrics_metrics.description: For each even d there exists a CW complex X_d which is simultaneously an example for all admissible coefficient rings R in the table; X_d can be chosen to have the simplest CW structure consistent with its cohomology, namely a single cell in each dimension a multiple of d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: X_2 = CP^∞, X_4 = HP^∞. Construction references: [SSAT] or [Hoffman & Porter 1973]. For certain p one must pick primes satisfying congruence conditions (e.g. for d=6 choose primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product property for polynomial cohomology rings
rubrics_metrics.description: The product of two spaces with polynomial cohomology is again a space with polynomial cohomology: H^*(X×Y;R) ≅ H^*(X;R)⊗_R H^*(Y;R) ≅ R[α_1,...,α_m,β_1,...,β_n], assuming the number of polynomial generators is finite in each degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Künneth formula / cross product; example: (CP^∞)^n has H^* ≅ Z[α_1,...,α_n] with each |α_i|=2. However, with Z and Z_p coefficients products of one-variable examples do not exhaust all possibilities (see §4.D for classification over Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free graded-commutative algebra single-generator classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-generator free graded commutative algebra is either a polynomial algebra R[α] on an even-dimension generator α, or the quotient R[α]/(2α^2) with α odd-dimensional. If R is a field, R[α]/(2α^2) is the exterior algebra R[α] when char(R)≠2 and the polynomial algebra R[α] when char(R)=2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Free’ means 'having no unnecessary relations'; in general a free graded-commutative algebra is a tensor product of single-generator free ones, and every graded-commutative algebra is a quotient of a free one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology rings of subcomplexes of the n-torus
rubrics_metrics.description: For the n-torus T^n with H^*(T^n;Z) the exterior algebra Z[α_1,...,α_n], if X ⊂ T^n is a subcomplex obtained by omitting certain cells then H^*(X;Z) is the quotient of Z[α_1,...,α_n] by the ideal generated by the monomials corresponding to the omitted cells (the minimal omitted cells generate the ideal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: viewing T^n as a quotient of the n-cube and intersecting with a hyperplane gives a simplicial complex CX; there is a one-to-one correspondence between subcomplexes X⊂T^n and simplicial subcomplexes CX. Classification result (Gubeladze 1998): the ring H^*(X;Z) (or even H^*(X;Z_2)) determines the subcomplex X uniquely up to permutation of circle factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Cohen–Macaulay cup-product rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: let X = CP^∞/CP^{n-1}. The induced map embeds H^*(X;Z) in Z[α] as the subring generated by 1, α^n, α^{n+1},..., and viewed as a module over Z[α^n] it is free with basis {1, α^{n+1},...,α^{2n-1}}. Thus H^*(X;Z) is Cohen–Macaulay: a ring containing a polynomial subring over which it is a finitely generated free module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohen–Macaulay cup-product rings occur frequently; polynomial rings are rarer. This provides an explicit family of nonfree but well-behaved cup-product rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold definition and local homology characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: An n-manifold is a Hausdorff space M in which each point has an open neighborhood homeomorphic to R^n. Equivalently, for x∈M the local homology H_i(M,M−{x};Z) is nonzero only for i=n (and H_n(M,M−{x};Z) ≈ Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This local homology formulation identifies the dimension intrinsically via excision and homotopy equivalence R^n−{0} ≃ S^{n−1}. Examples: closed manifolds are compact manifolds without boundary; S^n, RP^n, CP^n are standard examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local orientation and global orientability (algebraic-topological definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orientation of R^n at a point x is a choice of generator of the infinite cyclic group H_n(R^n,R^n−{x}). A local orientation of an n-manifold M at x is a choice µ_x ∈ H_n(M||x). A global orientation of M is a function x↦µ_x assigning to each x a local orientation such that each x has a neighborhood B for which all µ_y (y∈B) are images of a single generator µ_B ∈ H_n(M||B). If such a consistent choice exists M is orientable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotations preserve the chosen generator, reflections reverse sign. Every manifold has a two-sheeted orientable cover M~; orientability corresponds to that cover having two components. The construction generalizes to R-orientability for an arbitrary coefficient ring R: an R-orientation chooses generators (units) of H_n(M||x;R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental class and its equivalence with R-orientability for closed manifolds
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental class for a closed n-manifold M with coefficients in R is an element µ∈H_n(M;R) whose image in H_n(M||x;R) is a generator for all x. Such a µ exists iff M is closed and R-orientable. Consequently H_n(M;Z) is Z if M is orientable and 0 otherwise; in either case H_n(M;Z_2)=Z_2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The image of a global fundamental class gives the section x↦µ_x that is an R-orientation. Conversely a global section of the covering MR→M whose values are generators gives a fundamental class; compactness of M follows from support of representing cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.26 (precise homology/cohomology consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a closed connected n-manifold. (a) If M is R-orientable, the map H_n(M;R)→H_n(M||x;R)≈R is an isomorphism for all x. (b) If M is not R-orientable, the map H_n(M;R)→H_n(M||x;R)≈R is injective with image {r∈R | 2r=0} for all x. (c) H_i(M;R)=0 for i>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, when R=Z this yields H_n(M;Z)=Z or 0 according to orientability, and for R=Z_2 always Z_2. The theorem follows from Lemma 3.27 via consideration of sections of MR→M and Mayer–Vietoris arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3.27 (sections imply classes on compact subsets and vanishing above dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be an n-manifold and A⊂M compact. (a) If x↦α_x is a section of the covering MR→M, then there is a unique class α_A∈H_n(M||A;R) whose image in H_n(M||x;R) is α_x for all x∈A. (b) H_i(M||A;R)=0 for i>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is proven by induction using Mayer–Vietoris: if true for A,B and A∩B then true for A∪B; use local balls to construct the classes; vanishing above dimension follows from excision and the local Euclidean structure. The lemma is the technical backbone for Theorem 3.26.
